tool.name: Swift
tool.tagline: Safe, fast, modern language for Apple platforms, servers and beyond
tool.description: Swift is Apple's open-source, compiled language with value types, optionals, protocols and generics, and a concurrency model that checks data races at compile time. It is the main language for iOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS apps and is also used on Linux servers. Learn it to build native Apple apps with SwiftUI and to write fast, safe code that the compiler helps you get right.

glossary.def: Apple's free app for writing, running and testing Swift code and building apps for iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices.
A page in Xcode (or the Swift Playgrounds app) where Swift code runs as you type and each line's result appears beside it; handy for learning and experiments.
A named value that can't change after it's set. In Swift you create one with let.
What happens when a calculation produces a number too big (or too small) for its type to hold, like adding 1 to the largest possible Int.
Swift's word for deliberately stopping the program with an error when something impossible happens, such as an overflow or reading past the end of an array, instead of carrying on with a wrong value.
What a person sees as one character, even when it's stored as several Unicode numbers, such as e plus an accent, or a flag emoji. Swift's Character type is one of these.
A type whose values are copied when assigned or passed, so each variable has its own independent value. In Swift, structs, enums, strings and arrays are value types.
A type whose values are shared, not copied: variables hold a reference to one object, so a change through one variable is seen through all. Swift classes, actors and closures are reference types.
A Swift range that includes both ends, written a...b: 1...3 means 1, 2 and 3.
A Swift range that stops just before its upper end, written a..<b: 0..<3 means 0, 1 and 2.
Covering every possible case. A Swift switch must be exhaustive, so the compiler complains if some value isn't handled.
Swift's guard condition else { ... } statement: it checks a requirement and, if it fails, must leave the current block right away.
A Swift type that may hold a value or nil (nothing), written with a question mark: String? is a String or nothing. You must unwrap it before use.
To check that a Swift optional isn't nil and take out the value inside, for example with if let.
Unwrapping a Swift optional with if let or guard let, which gives you a plain, non-optional name for the value when it exists.
Swift's ?? operator: a ?? b gives the value inside the optional a, or b if a is nil.
Following several steps through optionals with ?., as in user?.address?.city; the whole result becomes nil as soon as any step is nil.
Taking the value out of a Swift optional with ! without checking; the program crashes if it's nil.
The name written before a value when calling a Swift function, like from: in move(from: 1, to: 5). It can differ from the name used inside the function.
A parameter that accepts any number of values, written with ... after the type in Swift: func sum(_ xs: Int...).
A Swift function parameter the function may change, with the change written back to the caller's variable. The caller passes it with &, as in double(&x).
The automatic names $0, $1, ... for a Swift closure's first, second, ... inputs, so you don't have to name them.
A closure written after a function call's brackets instead of inside them, as in names.map { $0.uppercased() }.
When a closure uses variables from the code around it, it captures them: it keeps using those same variables, and keeps them alive, even after that code has finished.
Square brackets at the start of a Swift closure, like [x] or [weak self], that say how it should capture particular values.
A closure that a function keeps to call after the function has returned, such as code to run when a download finishes. Swift requires such parameters to be marked @escaping.
A property that holds its own value inside each instance, like x and y in a Point struct.
The code (init in Swift) that creates a new instance of a type and gives all its properties their starting values.
The initializer Swift writes for a struct automatically, with one argument per stored property, like Point(x: 1, y: 2).
A method of a Swift struct or enum that changes the value it belongs to. It must be marked mutating and can only be called on a var.
Code in a Swift class (deinit) that runs just before an instance is removed from memory, used for clean-up.
A helper initializer in a Swift class that must hand off to another initializer of the same class; the main ones that set every property are called designated initializers.
In Swift, a named list of requirements (properties and methods) that any struct, class or enum can promise to provide, so code can work with any type that has those abilities.
A Swift type conforms to a protocol when it provides everything the protocol requires and declares that it does, as in struct Square: Shape.
A Swift extension on a protocol that gives every conforming type ready-made methods and default versions of requirements.
A Swift block (extension TypeName { ... }) that adds methods, computed properties, initializers or protocol conformances to an existing type, even one you didn't write.
A Swift type written any P: a box that can hold a value of any type conforming to protocol P, with the actual type able to change from value to value.
A Swift type written some P: one specific type conforming to P that the compiler knows but hides from the caller, such as SwiftUI's some View.
Choosing which function to call while compiling, based on the type the code declares. It's fast and allows further optimisation.
Choosing which version of a method to call while the program runs, based on the actual type of the value; slightly slower but needed when the type isn't known in advance.
A fixed number or string attached to each case of a Swift enum, like mercury = 1, which lets you turn cases into plain values and back.
Extra data carried by a particular Swift enum case, like the last four digits in case card(last4: String). Each case can carry different data.
A property that stores nothing itself and works out its value each time it is read, like area from width and height.
Code attached to a Swift stored property (willSet or didSet) that runs just before or after the property's value changes.
A Swift property (lazy var) whose starting value isn't worked out until the first time it is used.
A property that belongs to the type itself rather than to each instance, declared with static, like Point.origin.
Rules that decide which other code may see and use a declaration, set with words such as private, internal and public.
Swift 6's throws(ErrorType) form, which says exactly which type of error a function can throw, so callers know what they may catch.
A requirement on a generic type parameter, such as T: Comparable, which limits the allowed types and lets the code use what they promise.
A placeholder type inside a Swift protocol (associatedtype Element) that each conforming type fills in, like the element type of a collection.
Extra conditions on generic types written after where, such as where T: Hashable, C.Element == Int.
The compiler making a separate, type-specific copy of generic code for a particular type, so it runs as fast as code written for that type.
A Swift protocol (Encodable plus Decodable) for types that can be converted to and from formats such as JSON; the compiler usually writes the conversion code for you.
A nested enum in a Codable Swift type that lists which properties to encode and decode, and which name each one uses in the data.
A Swift function marked async that can pause while waiting for something slow, like the network, letting other work run; you call it with await.
A place marked with await where a Swift async function may pause, let other work run, and continue later.
In Swift, a unit of asynchronous work you can start, wait for and cancel; Task { ... } starts one from ordinary code.
Organising concurrent work so that child tasks live inside a parent's scope: the parent waits for its children, errors flow up, and cancelling the parent cancels the children.
A task started inside another task (with async let or a task group) that must finish before its parent's scope ends.
A Swift tool (withTaskGroup) for starting any number of child tasks and collecting their results as each one finishes.
Cancelling a Swift task only sets a flag; the task's own code must check it and stop, which Swift's built-in waiting functions do for you.
A Swift reference type that protects its data by letting only one task at a time run its code; other code must await to use it.
In Swift concurrency, which actor (if any) a piece of code belongs to, and so which data it may touch without waiting.
A region of a Swift program whose data is protected together: one actor, the main actor, or a single task. Data may only be shared between domains safely.
The Swift global actor that runs code on the main thread, where all user interface work must happen; marked with @MainActor.
An actor that code in many different types can belong to, marked with an attribute like @MainActor.
For Swift actors: while one of an actor's methods is paused at an await, other calls to the same actor may run, so its data can change in the meantime.
A Swift keyword marking a member of an actor-isolated type as not belonging to that actor, so it can be used without await but must not touch the actor's changeable data.
A Swift protocol for types whose values are safe to share between concurrently running code, such as structs of simple values and actors.
A setting that picks which version's rules the Swift compiler applies; in Swift 6 mode possible data races are compile errors instead of warnings.
A Swift 6 compiler check that allows passing a non-Sendable value to other concurrent code when it can prove the sender never uses that value again.
Automatic Reference Counting: Swift counts how many strong references point to each class instance and frees the instance the moment the count reaches zero.
A normal reference to a Swift class instance, which keeps the instance alive as long as the reference exists.
A reference (weak var) that doesn't keep an object alive; it automatically becomes nil when the object is freed.
A Swift reference that doesn't keep an object alive and is never nil; using it after the object has been freed crashes.
Two or more objects holding strong references to each other, so their counts never reach zero and they are never freed: a memory leak.
A Swift type marked ~Copyable whose values can't be copied: each has exactly one owner, and assigning it moves it instead.
Which part of a program is responsible for a value and when it is destroyed; Swift's borrowing and consuming keywords say whether a function only uses a value or takes it over.
A Swift type marked @propertyWrapper that packages the logic for storing a property, applied with an attribute like @Clamped or SwiftUI's @State.
An extra value a Swift property wrapper offers, reached by writing $ before the property name, like $count for a @State property.
A Swift feature (@resultBuilder) that turns a list of statements in a closure into one combined value; SwiftUI uses it to build views from a plain list.
A Swift macro written with # that stands on its own and produces an expression or declarations, like #expect(...).
A Swift macro written with @ in front of a declaration, adding code to it, like @Observable on a class.
The tree structure a compiler builds from source code, where each node is a piece of the code such as a function, statement or expression.
Apple's Swift library for reading and creating Swift source code as a syntax tree; macro implementations are built with it.
Swift's built-in tool for building code, running tests and downloading the packages a project depends on, configured in a Package.swift file.
The file at the top of a Swift package, written in Swift, that lists the package's name, its products, targets and dependencies.
Swift's modern built-in testing library: test functions are marked @Test and checks are written with #expect.
A table the Swift runtime keeps for each type's conformance to a protocol, listing where that type's implementations of the protocol's requirements are.
A Swift build setting that lets the compiler look at all files of a module together, so it can make more calls faster.
A debug build is compiled for easy debugging, with few speed optimisations; a release build is fully optimised and is what users get. Measure speed only on release builds.
Apple's framework for building app screens in Swift by describing what the interface should look like; views are structs and update automatically when data changes.
A group of statements between curly braces { }, such as the body of an if, a loop or a function, that runs together.
A line of code that introduces a new name — a constant, variable, function or type — and says what it is.
In SwiftUI, a piece of the user interface, such as a button, a text label or a whole screen, described by a struct that conforms to the View protocol.

concepts.name: Constants, variables and types
concepts.summary: Write your first Swift code: name values with let and var, let Swift work out their types, and use the basic types.
concepts.why: Every Swift program is built from named values and their types, and Swift's let-first style keeps code predictable.
concepts.body:
A program is a list of instructions for a computer, written in a **programming language** such as Swift. The text you write is called **source code**. Before it runs, a tool called the **compiler** checks it and translates it into the computer's own instructions; this step is called **compiling**.

To try Swift on a Mac, use **Xcode**, Apple's free app for writing Swift, and open a **playground**: a page where your code runs as you type and each result appears beside it. On Linux or Windows, install Swift from swift.org and run a file with `swift main.swift` in a terminal.

Programs keep values under names. `let name = "Ana"` creates a **constant**: a named value that never changes. `var score = 0` creates a **variable**, whose value you can change later: `score = 10`. Swift style is to use `let` by default and `var` only when the value really changes.

Every value has a **data type** (its type), which says what kind of value it is. The basic ones:

- `Int` holds an **integer**, a whole number: 42, -7.
- `Double` holds a **floating-point number**, one with a decimal point: 9.99. `Float` is a less precise version.
- `Bool` holds a **boolean**: `true` or `false`.
- `String` holds a **string** of text, `"hello"`; `Character` holds a single character.

You rarely have to write types. In `let count = 3`, Swift sees a whole number and makes `count` an `Int`; this is **type inference**. To choose a type yourself, add a **type annotation** after a colon: `let ratio: Float = 0.5`. A name's type never changes afterwards. Swift is **statically typed**: the compiler checks every type before the program runs, so mix-ups are caught early.

Swift never converts between number types on its own: adding an `Int` to a `Double` is an error. Do a **type conversion** yourself by writing the type's name like an instruction: `Double(count)`. `Int(9.99)` cuts off the decimal part and gives 9.

Each number type has a largest value. Going past it is an **overflow**, and Swift deliberately stops the program (it **traps**) rather than quietly giving a wrong answer: `Int.max + 1` crashes. The operators `&+`, `&-` and `&*` wrap around instead, for when that's what you want.

`print(name, score)` shows values, separated by spaces.
concepts.code:
let name = "Swift"          // String, worked out by Swift
var version = 6             // Int
let pi: Double = 3.14159    // type written explicitly
version += 1                // var can change: now 7

let total = Double(version) * pi   // convert Int to Double first
print(name, version)        // Swift 7
print(Int(total))           // 21 (decimal part cut off)

let big = Int8.max          // 127: Int8 is a small integer type
print(big &+ 1)             // -128 (&+ wraps around on purpose)
// print(big + 1)           // would crash: too big for Int8
takeaways: Prefer `let`; use `var` only for values that change
Swift never converts number types for you — write `Double(x)` or `Int(y)`
Going past a number type's limit stops the program; `&+` and friends wrap on purpose
pitfalls: Expecting `Int(2.9)` to round — it cuts off to 2; use `.rounded()` first.

quiz.q: What happens when you compile `let a = 2; let b = 1.5; let c = a + b`?
options: Compile error: Int and Double can't be added without conversion
quiz.explain: a is inferred as Int and b as Double, and Swift never converts number types on its own.

quiz.q: You write `let total = 5` and later `total = 6`. What happens?
options: Swift makes total a var automatically
The compiler reports an error, because a let constant can't change
quiz.explain: let creates a constant; to change a value later, declare it with var.

concepts.name: Strings and interpolation
concepts.summary: Build text with string interpolation and multi-line strings, and see why Swift counts characters the way people see them.
concepts.why: Text is everywhere in apps, and Swift's careful handling of characters explains why you can't grab a letter with a plain number like s[3].
concepts.body:
A `String` holds text, written in double quotes. To put a value inside text, use **string interpolation**: wrap it in `\(` and `)`, as in `"Hi \(name)"`. Any calculation can go inside: `"\(items * 2) points"`.

Text that runs over several lines goes between triple quotes, `"""`. Swift removes the indentation that matches the closing `"""`, so you can indent the text neatly along with your code.

Strings are **value types**: giving a string to another name, or passing it somewhere, hands over a separate copy. No other code can change your string behind your back. (Swift keeps this cheap by sharing the text until one copy actually changes.)

Computers store text as numbers. The **Unicode** standard gives every character in every language its own number, and Swift stores those numbers using **UTF-8**, as **bytes** — small numbers from 0 to 255. Plain English letters take one byte; other characters take several.

Some characters are even built from several Unicode numbers: `é` can be an `e` plus an accent mark, and a flag emoji is two special letters combined. Swift's `Character` type is what a person sees as one character, however it's stored; Swift calls this an **extended grapheme cluster**.

So `"café".count` is 4, even though it takes 5 bytes. The catch: to find the fourth character, Swift has to walk through the text from the start, so you can't write `s[3]` with a plain number. Positions use the type `String.Index` instead: `s.index(s.startIndex, offsetBy: 3)`, or methods like `firstIndex(of:)`.

Handy tools:

- `hasPrefix`, `hasSuffix`, `contains`, `lowercased()`, `split(separator:)`.
- `s.isEmpty` is faster and clearer than `s.count == 0`.
- Taking part of a string gives a `Substring`, which shares memory with the original. Turn it into a `String` with `String(part)` before keeping it for long.

For work on the raw bytes, use `word.utf8`, which presents the text as its UTF-8 bytes: `word.utf8.count`.
concepts.code:
let user = "Ana"
let items = 3
print("Hi \(user), you have \(items * 2) points")  // Hi Ana, you have 6 points

let word = "café"
print(word.count)           // 4 characters
print(word.utf8.count)      // 5 bytes

let i = word.index(word.startIndex, offsetBy: 3)
print(word[i])              // é

let csv = "a,b,c"
let parts = csv.split(separator: ",")   // three Substrings
print(parts.map { String($0).uppercased() })  // ["A", "B", "C"] (map: see Closures)

let poem = """
    Roses are red
    Swift is fast
    """
print(poem.hasPrefix("Roses"))  // true
takeaways: Put values into text with `\(value)`
`count` counts characters as people see them, not bytes
Use `String.Index`, not an `Int`, for positions; turn a `Substring` into a `String` to keep it
pitfalls: Keeping a small `Substring` of a huge string, which keeps the whole original text alive.

quiz.q: Why can't you write `name[2]` with a plain number in Swift?
options: Only arrays can be read by position
A character can take several bytes, so finding position 2 means walking through the text
quiz.explain: A Character can span several bytes, so Swift makes finding positions explicit with String.Index.

concepts.name: if, switch and loops
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if and switch, repeat work with for-in and while loops over ranges, and exit early with guard.
concepts.why: Every program chooses between actions and repeats steps; Swift's switch and guard are used constantly and are stricter than in many languages.
concepts.body:
Code normally runs from top to bottom. **if** runs some code only when a condition is true; this is a **conditional**: `if score > 50 { print("pass") } else { print("fail") }`. The condition must be a real `Bool`; Swift won't treat a number as true or false the way some languages do. Brackets around the condition are optional, but the braces `{ }` are required.

A **loop** repeats code. `for item in list { }` runs once for each element of a list, or of anything else Swift can step through. A **closed range**, `1...5`, counts 1 to 5 including 5; a **half-open range**, `0..<5`, counts 0 to 4, stopping before 5. `stride(from:to:by:)` counts in other steps. `while` repeats as long as a condition is true, and `repeat { } while` checks the condition after each pass.

**switch** compares a value with a list of `case`s and runs the first that matches; then it's done, with no `break` needed. One `case` can match several values (`case "a", "e":`), a range (`case 90...:` means 90 or more), or take the value with `let` and test it with `where`. A switch must be **exhaustive**: it has to cover every possible value, so you add `default:` for "anything else".

`guard condition else { return }` checks a requirement up front and leaves early if it fails. The `else` part must exit the current **scope** — the block of code between braces it sits in — with `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue`, and the compiler checks this. The **guard statement** keeps the main path of your code from being buried inside nested `if`s.

Since Swift 5.9, `if` and `switch` can also produce a value: `let label = if score > 50 { "pass" } else { "fail" }`.

In loops, `break` stops early and `continue` skips to the next pass. To leave an outer loop from inside an inner one, label it (`outer: for ...`) and write `break outer`.
takeaways: `switch` must cover every case and never carries on into the next one
`guard ... else` exits early and keeps the main path flat
`..<` stops before the end; `...` includes it
pitfalls: Expecting a switch case to carry on into the next one, as in some older languages — in Swift each case ends by itself.

quiz.q: What must the `else` block of a `guard` statement do?
options: Exit the current scope (return, throw, break or continue)
quiz.explain: The compiler enforces that control can't continue past a failed guard.

concepts.name: Optionals
concepts.summary: Represent values that may be missing with optionals, and unwrap them safely with if let, guard let, ?? and optional chaining.
concepts.why: Using a missing value by mistake is one of the most common causes of crashes; optionals make the compiler check for it, and almost every Swift API uses them.
concepts.body:
Sometimes a value may be missing: a user may have no nickname, and turning the text "abc" into a number fails. Many languages use a special empty value, `nil` or **null**, for this, and programs crash when they use it by mistake.

In Swift a normal type can never be `nil`. To allow a missing value you use an **optional**: `String?` means "a String, or nothing". Behind the scenes it's a simple type with two possibilities: some value, or none.

You can't use an optional as if it were the value. First you **unwrap** it: check that it isn't `nil` and take the value out.

- `if let name { ... }` runs the block only when `name` has a value, and inside it `name` is a plain `String`. This is **optional binding**.
- `guard let user else { return }` unwraps for the rest of the block, leaving early if the value is missing.
- `value ?? fallback` gives a default when the value is missing; `??` is the **nil-coalescing operator**.
- `user?.address?.city` is **optional chaining**: it follows each step, and the whole thing becomes `nil` as soon as any part is `nil`.

The **force unwrap** `value!` takes the value out without checking, and crashes if it's `nil`. Use it only when `nil` would mean a mistake in your own code, never for things like user input.

Many tools return optionals to say "that didn't work": `Int("42")` gives an `Int?` because the text might not be a number, and `list.first` is `nil` for an empty list. In older Apple code you'll also see types like `String!`, which unwrap themselves automatically and crash if nil; avoid them in new code.
concepts.code:
let typed = "42"
let number = Int(typed)          // Int?: the text might not be a number
if let number {
    print(number * 2)            // 84
}

let port = Int("8080") ?? 80     // 8080
let bad = Int("abc") ?? 80       // 80: "abc" isn't a number

var nickname: String? = nil
print(nickname?.count as Any)    // nil: the chain stopped early
nickname = "Mo"
print(nickname?.count ?? 0)      // 2

let word: String? = "hi"
print(word!)                     // hi (force unwrap: would crash if nil)
takeaways: `T?` may be nil; a plain `T` never is
Unwrap with `if let`, `guard let`, `??` or `?.`
`!` crashes on nil — use it only when nil would be a bug in your own code
pitfalls: Adding `!` just to make the compiler stop complaining; the crash just happens later, while the app runs.

quiz.q: `nickname` is a `String?`. What is the type of `nickname?.count`?
quiz.explain: Optional chaining makes the result optional, because the chain stops if nickname is nil.

quiz.q: Which expression gives 0 when `s` cannot be turned into an Int?
quiz.explain: The nil-coalescing operator ?? supplies a default when the optional is nil.

concepts.name: Arrays, dictionaries and sets
concepts.summary: Keep groups of values in arrays, dictionaries and sets, and transform them with map, filter and reduce.
concepts.why: Collections hold almost all of an app's data, and Swift copies them on assignment, unlike many other languages.
concepts.body:
Programs work with groups of values. Swift has three main kinds:

- An **array**, written `[Int]`, keeps values in order. Each value has a position number, its **index**, counting from 0 (**zero-based indexing**): `scores[0]` is the first.
- A **dictionary**, written `[String: Int]`, stores **key-value pairs**: you look a value up by its key, like a word in a real dictionary. Keys must be `Hashable`, meaning Swift can turn them into a quick lookup number; text and numbers are.
- A **set**, `Set<String>`, holds unique values in no particular order and answers "is this in it?" very fast.

Declared with `let`, a collection can't change at all. With `var` you can `append`, `insert`, `remove(at:)` and replace elements: `scores[0] = 100`.

Collections are **value types**: `var b = a` gives `b` its own copy, so changing `b` never changes `a`. Swift keeps this cheap by sharing the data until one of them changes.

Reading an array index that doesn't exist crashes the program. Use `first` or `last` (both optionals), or check `indices.contains(i)` when unsure. Looking up a dictionary key also returns an optional, because the key may be missing; `counts[word, default: 0] += 1` is the usual way to count things.

Collections have methods that take a small piece of code in braces — a closure — and run it for each element. Inside, `$0` stands for the current element: `scores.filter { $0 >= 70 }` keeps the passing scores. The common ones are `map` (change each element), `filter` (keep some), `reduce` (combine all into one value), `compactMap` (change each and leave out the nils), `sorted(by:)`, `contains(where:)` and `first(where:)`. The Closures lesson explains the braces in detail.

Loop over a dictionary with `for (key, value) in dict`, and over an array with positions using `for (i, x) in array.enumerated()`. Sets offer `union`, `intersection`, `subtracting` and `isSubset(of:)`.
concepts.code:
var scores = [72, 95, 88]
scores.append(60)
let passed = scores.filter { $0 >= 70 }      // [72, 95, 88]
let total = scores.reduce(0, +)              // 315: adds them all up

var copy = scores
copy[0] = 0
print(scores[0], copy[0])                    // 72 0 (copy is separate)

let words = ["a", "b", "a", "c", "a"]
var counts: [String: Int] = [:]              // empty dictionary
for w in words { counts[w, default: 0] += 1 }
print(counts["a"] ?? 0)                      // 3
print(counts["z"] as Any)                    // nil

let tags: Set = ["swift", "ios"]
print(tags.contains("ios"))                  // true
print(tags.union(["mac"]).count)             // 3
takeaways: Arrays, dictionaries and sets are copied on assignment
A dictionary lookup returns an optional; use `[k, default: v]` to count
Reading past the end of an array crashes
pitfalls: Assuming a dictionary or set keeps the order you added things in — it doesn't.

quiz.q: `var a = [1, 2]; var b = a; b.append(3)` — what is `a.count`?
quiz.explain: Arrays are value types, so b is a separate copy and a keeps its two elements.

concepts.name: Functions and argument labels
concepts.summary: Write functions with argument labels, default values, any number of inputs, inout parameters, and several results at once.
concepts.why: Functions let you name a piece of work and reuse it, and Swift's argument labels shape how all Swift code reads.
concepts.body:
A **function** is a named piece of work you can run again and again, like a recipe. You declare it with `func`:

```swift
func greet(name: String) -> String {
    return "Hello, \(name)"
}
```

`name` is a **parameter**: a named input with a type. `-> String` says what the function hands back, its **return value**, which `return` sends out. Call it with `greet(name: "Ana")`; the value you pass in, `"Ana"`, is the **argument**.

Each parameter has an **argument label**, used when calling, and a parameter name, used inside. Usually they're the same, but they can differ — `func move(from start: Int, to end: Int)` is called as `move(from: 1, to: 5)` — or you can leave the label out with `_`: `func square(_ x: Int)` is called as `square(4)`. Labels make calls read like sentences, and Apple's guidelines ask you to name things so each call reads clearly.

More features:

- A **default value** lets callers leave a parameter out: `func greet(_ name: String, loud: Bool = false)`.
- A **variadic** parameter, `func sum(_ xs: Int...)`, accepts any number of values and receives them as an array.
- Parameters are constants inside the function. An **inout** parameter can be changed, and the caller marks its variable with `&`: `swap(&a, &b)`.
- Return several values at once as a **tuple**, a small group of values: `-> (min: Int, max: Int)`.
- If the body is a single expression, you can leave out `return`.
- Two functions may share a name if their parameter types or labels differ; this is **overloading**.

When a call's result is ignored, the compiler warns you; mark a function `@discardableResult` when ignoring its result is normal.

Functions are values too: their type looks like `(Int, Int) -> Int`, and you can store them in variables, pass them to other functions and return them.
takeaways: Argument label (used when calling) vs parameter name (used inside); `_` removes the label
Default values, variadic parameters, and `inout` with `&`
Return a tuple for several results
pitfalls: Using `inout` where returning a new value would be clearer — it makes code harder to follow.

quiz.q: Given `func move(from start: Int, to end: Int)`, how is it called?
quiz.explain: The argument labels from and to are used at the call site; start and end are internal names.

concepts.name: Closures
concepts.summary: Write closures — functions without a name — shorten them with trailing-closure and $0 syntax, and understand capturing and @escaping.
concepts.why: Closures power collection methods, code that runs when something finishes, and SwiftUI, so you'll read them in nearly every Swift file.
concepts.body:
A **closure** is a function without a name, written right where it's needed, usually to hand to another function. `names.sorted(by: { (a: String, b: String) -> Bool in a < b })` passes a closure that tells `sorted` how to compare two names. The word `in` separates the inputs from the body.

Swift lets you shorten that a lot:

- Types can be worked out from context: `{ a, b in a < b }`.
- A closure with a single expression returns it automatically.
- `$0` and `$1` are **shorthand argument names** for the first and second inputs: `{ $0 < $1 }`.
- An operator can stand in for the whole closure: `sorted(by: <)`.
- A **trailing closure** goes after the brackets when it's the last argument: `names.map { $0.uppercased() }`. Several trailing closures can follow, the later ones with labels.

A closure holds on to the variables it uses from the surrounding code: it keeps using those very variables, not copies, and keeps them alive. Swift says the closure has **captured** them. A counter closure that adds to a captured `var` remembers its count between calls. To keep a copy of a value as it is right now instead, list it in a **capture list**, square brackets at the start: `{ [x] in ... }`.

By default, a closure passed to a function can only be used before that function returns. If the function keeps the closure to call later — say, code to run when a download finishes — its parameter must be marked `@escaping`. Such an **escaping closure** can accidentally keep things alive forever; a later lesson shows how to prevent that.

Closures are shared, not copied: two variables holding the same closure share whatever it captured.
concepts.code:
let names = ["Zoe", "adam", "Maya"]
let sorted = names.sorted { $0.lowercased() < $1.lowercased() }
print(sorted)                       // ["adam", "Maya", "Zoe"]

func makeCounter() -> () -> Int {
    var count = 0
    return { count += 1; return count }   // captures count
}
let next = makeCounter()
_ = next()
print(next())                       // 2

var handlers: [() -> Void] = []     // an array of closures
func register(_ h: @escaping () -> Void) { handlers.append(h) }

var level = 1
register { [level] in print("captured", level) }   // value right now
register { print("live", level) }                  // the variable itself
level = 5
handlers.forEach { $0() }           // captured 1, live 5
takeaways: Trailing closures and `$0` keep calls short
Closures use the captured variables themselves — use `[x]` to keep a copy of the current value
A closure kept to run later must be `@escaping`
pitfalls: Writing long closures full of `$0` and `$1`; name the inputs once it's longer than a line or two.

quiz.q: Why must a closure that a function stores in an array be marked @escaping?
options: It is used after the function that received it has returned
quiz.explain: @escaping means the closure may be called after the function returns, which storing it allows.

concepts.name: Structures and value semantics
concepts.summary: Describe your own kinds of data with structs: stored properties, the automatic initializer, methods and mutating.
concepts.why: Structs are Swift's default way to describe your own data; most SwiftUI views and data models are structs.
concepts.body:
Real things have several details: a point has an x and a y; a user has a name and an age. A **struct** groups named values into a new type of your own: `struct Point { var x: Double; var y: Double }`. The values inside, `x` and `y`, are its **stored properties**, and one value made from the type is an **instance**.

The code that creates an instance is an **initializer**, and Swift writes one for you: `Point(x: 1, y: 2)`. This **memberwise initializer** takes one argument per property, as long as you don't write your own `init` inside the struct.

Structs are **value types**: assigning or passing one makes a copy, so each variable owns its own data and no other code can change your copy. Most of Swift's own types — `Int`, `String`, arrays, dictionaries — are structs.

Functions written inside a type are **methods**, called with a dot: `a.distance(to: b)`. Inside a method, `self` means the instance it was called on; you rarely need to write it.

A method that changes the struct's properties must be marked **`mutating`**, and can only be called on a `var`. An instance stored in a `let` can't change at all, even properties declared with `var`.

`static` makes a property or method that belongs to the type itself rather than to each instance: `static let origin = Point(x: 0, y: 0)` is used as `Point.origin`.

Swift also has classes (next lesson). Apple's advice: start with a struct, and use a class only when several parts of the program must share one and the same object.

Writing `: Equatable` after the name makes Swift write `==` for you, so two points can be compared. Promising abilities like this is done with protocols, covered later.
takeaways: Structs are copied on assignment — each variable owns its value
Methods that change properties need `mutating`
Start with a struct; use a class when several parts must share one object
pitfalls: Writing your own `init` inside the struct body and losing the automatic memberwise initializer (an extension, covered later, lets you keep both).

quiz.q: `let p = Point(x: 1, y: 1)` — can you call the mutating method `p.move(dx: 1, dy: 0)`?
options: No, a let struct instance is entirely immutable
Yes, because x is declared var
Yes, but only inside a class
quiz.explain: A let constant holding a struct can't be changed, so mutating methods are not allowed on it.

concepts.name: Classes and reference semantics
concepts.summary: Use classes for objects that are shared rather than copied: initializers, inheritance, overriding, and identity checks with ===.
concepts.why: Many Apple frameworks are built on classes, and because classes are shared rather than copied they cause a classic family of bugs.
concepts.body:
A **class** looks like a struct, but it's a **reference type**. A class instance lives in one place in memory, and variables hold a **reference** to it — like several people holding the address of the same house. Assigning or passing it copies the reference, not the object, so a change made through one variable shows up through all of them. `===` checks whether two variables refer to the very same instance.

Other differences from structs:

- There's no automatic memberwise initializer: you write an `init` that sets every stored property (unless it has a default value).
- Methods may change properties without `mutating`, even through a `let`. For a class, `let` only fixes *which* object the constant refers to.
- A **deinitializer**, `deinit { }`, runs just before the object is thrown away, once nothing refers to it anymore. Swift keeps track of that automatically; a later lesson explains how.

A class can build on another: `class Dog: Animal` gets all of Animal's properties and methods. This is **inheritance**, and Dog is a **subclass** of Animal. To replace an inherited method, **override** it with the `override` keyword, and call the original version through `super`. Marking a class or method `final` forbids this, which also lets Swift make its calls a little faster.

Setting up a subclass has rules: first set the subclass's own properties, then call `super.init(...)` so the parent can set up its part. A **convenience initializer** is a helper that must call another `init` of the same class, and `required init` forces every subclass to provide that initializer.

Use a class when something has an identity that several parts of the program share — a network connection, the data behind a screen, a cache. Mark it `final` unless you mean it to be subclassed.
takeaways: Classes are shared, not copied; `===` checks whether two refer to the same instance
A subclass sets its own properties before calling `super.init`
Mark classes `final` unless designed to be subclassed
pitfalls: Passing a class instance to several places and being surprised that a change shows up everywhere.

quiz.q: `let acc = Account(owner: "A")` — is `acc.deposit(10)` allowed, given deposit changes balance?
options: No, acc is a let constant
Only if deposit is marked mutating
Yes, let only fixes which instance acc refers to
quiz.explain: For a class, let fixes which instance acc refers to, not the contents of that object.

concepts.name: Enumerations and associated values
concepts.summary: Define enums with a fixed set of options, raw values and associated values, and handle every case with switch.
concepts.why: Enums describe "one of these options" precisely, and the compiler checks that your code handles every option.
concepts.body:
Often a value must be one of a few fixed options: a direction is north, south, east or west. An **enum** (short for enumeration) defines such a type: `enum Direction { case north, south, east, west }`. Each option is a case. When Swift already knows the type, you can skip its name: `let d: Direction = .north`.

An enum can give each case a **raw value** of one type: `enum Planet: Int { case mercury = 1, venus }` makes venus 2. `Planet(rawValue: 3)` turns a number back into a case, but it returns an optional, because the number might not match any case. With `String` raw values, each case's name is its default raw value. Add `: CaseIterable` to get a list of every case, `Planet.allCases`.

More powerful are **associated values**: each case can carry its own extra data, of any type.

```swift
enum Payment {
    case cash
    case card(last4: String)
    case transfer(iban: String, amount: Double)
}
```

You take the data out in a `switch`: `case .card(let last4):` or `case let .transfer(iban, amount):`. A switch over an enum must handle every case, so when you add a case later, the compiler points at every switch that needs updating — a big reason to describe states with enums rather than separate true/false flags.

Enums can have their own properties and methods (a method that changes the case is marked `mutating`). `if case .card(let n) = payment { }` checks for just one case. `indirect` allows an enum that contains itself, such as a tree of calculations.

Swift's own optionals are an enum, `Optional`, with two possibilities: `.some(value)`, whose associated value is the value, and `.none`.
takeaways: Associated values attach different data to each case
A `switch` over an enum must cover every case — the compiler finds missing ones
`Enum(rawValue:)` returns an optional
pitfalls: Adding `default:` to every enum switch, which stops the compiler pointing out each new case.

quiz.q: What does `Planet(rawValue: 42)` return when no case has raw value 42?
options: nil, because it returns an optional
quiz.explain: Creating a case from a raw value returns an optional, because the value may not match any case.

concepts.name: Computed properties and observers
concepts.summary: Use computed properties, lazy properties and property observers, and make a property readable everywhere but changeable only inside.
concepts.why: Properties are how Swift types expose state; observers and computed values replace most getter and setter methods.
concepts.body:
**Stored properties** hold values (see Structures). A **computed property** stores nothing: it works out its value each time it's read, and can optionally have a setter — code that runs when you assign to it:

```swift
var area: Double { width * height }
```

A read-only computed property can omit `get`. With a setter, the new value arrives as `newValue`.

**Property observers** run code around changes to a stored property: `willSet` sees `newValue` before the change, `didSet` sees `oldValue` after it. They're handy for checking values, logging, or updating other properties that depend on this one. Observers do not fire during the type's own initializer.

**Lazy** properties (`lazy var`) aren't computed until first accessed — useful for expensive setup that may not be needed. They must be `var`, and if several threads (parts of a program running at the same time) touch one at once, it may be set up twice.

**Type properties** belong to the type itself and use `static` (or `class`, in a class, for computed ones a subclass may override).

**Access control** — keywords such as `private` that limit which code may use something — can differ for reading and writing: `private(set) var count = 0` can be read wherever the type is visible but changed only inside it. This is the usual way to show data to others without letting them change it.

Read-only computed properties can also be marked `throws` (may fail with an error; see Errors) or `async` (may wait for slow work; see async/await): `var avatar: Image { get async throws { ... } }`.

Prefer a computed property over a method when the value is cheap, has no side effects and reads like an attribute.
takeaways: Computed properties calculate on each read; observers react to writes
`private(set)` lets others read a property only the type itself can change
`lazy var` defers expensive setup until first use
pitfalls: Doing heavy work in a computed property that callers assume is cheap.

quiz.q: When does a `didSet` observer NOT run?
options: When the new value equals the old one
When the type is a class
When the property is set inside the type's own initializer
quiz.explain: Observers are skipped while an initializer sets the property of its own type.

concepts.name: Protocols
concepts.summary: Define protocols with property and method requirements, conform types to them, and add default implementations.
concepts.why: Much of Swift is built on protocols: comparing values, saving data as JSON, safe concurrency and every SwiftUI screen all rely on them.
concepts.body:
A **protocol** is a list of requirements — properties, methods, initializers — without the code for them. Any struct, class or enum can **conform** to it by providing them:

```swift
protocol Shape {
    var area: Double { get }
    func describe() -> String
}
```

Property requirements say only `{ get }` or `{ get set }`; a stored or computed property can satisfy them. Method requirements that modify a value type are marked `mutating`.

Protocols can be used as types: `let shapes: [any Shape]` holds a mix of different conforming types. The word `any` marks a box that can hold any conforming value (an existential type, covered later).

A **protocol extension** — an `extension` block (next lesson) written for a protocol — adds ready-made methods, and default versions of requirements, to every conforming type. This is how the standard library gives every `Collection` methods like `map`, `contains` and `isEmpty` from just a few requirements.

Protocols can inherit from others (`protocol Named: CustomStringConvertible`), be composed (`Shape & Named`), and be limited to classes with `AnyObject` (needed for the `weak` references of the ARC lesson).

For many standard protocols the compiler writes the conformance code for you: `Equatable`, `Hashable`, `Comparable` (for enums), `Codable`.

A subtle point: a method that exists only in a protocol extension (not as a requirement) uses **static dispatch** — Swift picks which version to run from the type written in the code, while compiling. So if a conforming type defines the same method, calls through `any Protocol` still run the extension's version. Make it a requirement to get **dynamic dispatch**, where the version is chosen from the actual value while the program runs.
takeaways: Protocols declare requirements; types of any kind can conform
Protocol extensions provide default implementations
Through `any P`, only requirements run the conforming type's own version
pitfalls: Expecting an override of an extension-only method to be called through the protocol type.

quiz.q: A method `hello()` exists only in `extension P` (not a requirement). Type `T: P` defines its own `hello()`. What does `(T() as any P).hello()` call?
quiz.explain: Extension-only methods use static dispatch: Swift picks the version from the type written in the code, here any P, so the extension's version runs.

concepts.name: Extensions
concepts.summary: Add methods, computed properties, initializers and protocol conformances to existing types with extensions.
concepts.why: Extensions keep code organised and let you add abilities to types you don't own, such as Int or String.
concepts.body:
An **extension** adds functionality to an existing type — including types you didn't write, like `Int`, `String` or `URL`:

```swift
extension Int {
    var isEven: Bool { self % 2 == 0 }
}
```

Extensions can add computed properties, methods (`mutating` on structs and enums), initializers, subscripts (the `[ ]` access you use on arrays), types nested inside, and **protocol conformances**. They cannot add stored properties or override existing members.

Two common uses:

- **Adding conformances after the fact**: make an existing type conform to your protocol, e.g. `extension Date: MyFormattable {}`. In Swift 6 the compiler warns when you conform a type you don't own to a protocol you don't own either; mark it `@retroactive` if you accept the risk of clashing with the owner later.
- **Code organization**: put each conformance in its own extension, `extension Profile: Codable { ... }`, so the file reads in sections.

Adding an initializer in an extension of a struct keeps the compiler-generated memberwise initializer, which a custom `init` in the main body would remove.

**Constrained extensions** add members only when a condition holds: `extension Array where Element: Numeric { func sum() -> Element { reduce(0, +) } }`. Here `sum()` exists only on arrays of numbers. (The Generics lesson explains `where`.)

Members added in extensions follow normal access control, and `private` members are visible to other extensions of the type in the same file.
takeaways: Extensions add behavior and conformances, not stored properties
Constrained extensions (`where Element: P`) add members conditionally
An `init` in an extension keeps the memberwise initializer
pitfalls: Adding broad extensions on standard types that clash with names from other modules.

quiz.q: Which of these can an extension NOT add?
quiz.explain: Extensions can't change how much data each instance stores, so stored properties aren't allowed.

concepts.name: Errors: throw, try and catch
concepts.summary: Throw and handle errors with do/catch, try?, try!, typed throws and the Result type.
concepts.why: File, network and data-decoding functions in Swift report failure by throwing errors, and you must handle them explicitly to call them.
takeaways: Mark failing functions `throws` and every call `try`
`try?` turns errors into nil; `try!` crashes
Typed throws `throws(E)` gives callers a concrete error type
pitfalls: Using `try?` everywhere and silently losing the reason something failed.

quiz.q: What does `try? parse("abc")` evaluate to if parse throws?
quiz.explain: try? converts any thrown error into a nil optional result.

concepts.name: Generics and constraints
concepts.summary: Write generic functions and types, limit their type parameters with protocols and where clauses, and use associated types.
concepts.why: Generics let one piece of code work for many types while the compiler still checks every type, just as Array and Dictionary do.
concepts.body:
A function using **generics** works with many types: its type parameters, in angle brackets, are placeholders the caller fills in: `func first<T>(_ xs: [T]) -> T?`. The compiler infers `T` at each call and checks types as if you'd written a specific version.

A **type constraint** says what a type parameter must support: `func largest<T: Comparable>(_ xs: [T]) -> T?` can use `<`. Longer requirements go in a **where clause**: `where T: Hashable, U.Element == T`.

Generic types work the same way: `struct Stack<Element> { private var items: [Element] = [] }`. Extensions can add members for specific constraints: `extension Stack where Element: Equatable`.

Protocols use an **associated type** instead of angle brackets: `Collection` has `associatedtype Element`. A conforming type fixes it, often by inference. You constrain associated types in generic code: `func sum<C: Collection>(_ c: C) -> Int where C.Element == Int`. Swift 5.7 added **primary associated types**, so you can write `some Collection<Int>` or `any Sequence<String>` directly.

The shorthand `func process(_ items: some Collection<Int>)` is equivalent to a generic parameter — it is the same as writing `<C: Collection<Int>>`.

When the compiler can see the real type, it makes a type-specific copy of the generic code — **specialization** — so generics are usually as fast as hand-written code. Across modules it may fall back to a slower general path unless the function is marked `@inlinable`.
takeaways: Type parameters plus constraints give reusable, type-safe code
Protocols use associated types; constrain them in `where` clauses
`some P<T>` in a parameter is shorthand for a generic parameter
pitfalls: Using `[Any]` or `any P` where a generic would keep full type information.

quiz.q: What does the constraint in `func f<T: Hashable>(_ x: T)` guarantee inside f?
options: Values of T can be hashed and compared with ==
quiz.explain: Hashable includes Equatable, so inside f you can compute a hash of T values and compare them with ==.

concepts.name: Codable and JSON
concepts.summary: Encode and decode JSON with Codable, JSONEncoder and JSONDecoder, CodingKeys and decoding strategies.
concepts.why: Almost every app talks to a JSON API, and Codable turns that into a few lines of type-safe code.
concepts.body:
Turning values into data such as JSON and back is called **serialization** (or encoding and decoding). `Codable` is another name for `Encodable & Decodable`. When all stored properties are themselves Codable, the compiler writes the encoding and decoding code for you — you just declare the conformance.

Decode with `JSONDecoder().decode(User.self, from: data)` and encode with `JSONEncoder().encode(value)`. Both throw on invalid or mismatched data, so they're called with `try`. The errors (`DecodingError.keyNotFound`, `.typeMismatch`...) describe exactly which path failed.

Mapping JSON to Swift:

- Optional properties may be missing or `null`; non-optional ones are required.
- Arrays and nested objects map to arrays and nested Codable types.
- Rename keys with a nested `enum CodingKeys: String, CodingKey { case id, fullName = "full_name" }` — every property you want coded must be listed.
- Or set `decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase` to map JSON names written like `full_name` to Swift names like `fullName` everywhere.
- Dates need a strategy, e.g. `decoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .iso8601`.
- `encoder.outputFormatting = [.prettyPrinted, .sortedKeys]` for readable output.

For unusual shapes, implement `init(from decoder: Decoder)` yourself using a container that reads values by key: `let c = try decoder.container(keyedBy: CodingKeys.self)` and `try c.decodeIfPresent(...)`.

Enums with raw values are Codable out of the box; enums with associated values get a synthesized keyed format.
takeaways: Declare `Codable` and the compiler writes the coding code
Rename keys with `CodingKeys` or a key strategy
Non-optional properties are required in the JSON
pitfalls: Declaring a field non-optional when the API sometimes omits it, so the whole decode fails.

quiz.q: A JSON object lacks the key for a non-optional `String` property. What happens on decode?
options: The property becomes an empty string
quiz.explain: Required (non-optional) properties must be present; their absence throws keyNotFound.

concepts.name: async/await and Task
concepts.summary: Write and call async functions that wait without blocking, start them from ordinary code with Task, and combine async with throws.
concepts.why: Networking, file access and most modern Apple APIs involve waiting, so this is how real apps do anything slow.
concepts.body:
Some work involves waiting: for the network, a file, a timer. An **async function** can pause while it waits without tying up a **thread** — one of the few lines of execution the computer runs side by side — so other work continues meanwhile. This style is called **asynchronous**. Mark the function `async` and call it with `await`:

```swift
func fetchUser(id: Int) async throws -> User
let user = try await fetchUser(id: 1)
```

Each `await` is a possible **suspension point**: other work may run before your function continues, and when it continues it may be on a different thread, unless it belongs to an actor (Actors lesson). Code between awaits runs without interruption from other tasks on the same actor.

You can only call async functions from other async code. To start async work from ordinary, **synchronous** code — a button tap, the start of a program — create a **Task**: `Task { await refresh() }`. A `Task` starts running immediately and keeps the actor and priority of the code that created it (for example the main actor, which runs user-interface code; see Actors). `let t = Task { ... }` lets you `await t.value` later or `t.cancel()`.

Combined with `throws`, the order is `async throws` in the declaration and `try await` at the call.

Foundation provides async APIs, e.g. `let (data, response) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url)`, and `try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(1))`.

Sequential `await`s run one after another. To run several things at the same time you need `async let` or task groups, covered in the next lesson, which also explains how to cancel async work.
takeaways: `async` functions suspend at each `await` without blocking a thread
`Task { }` starts async work from synchronous code
Write `async throws`, call with `try await`
pitfalls: Assuming state is unchanged after an `await` — other code may have run meanwhile.

quiz.q: What does `await` mark in Swift?
options: A place where a new thread is created
A blocking wait on the current thread
A possible suspension point where other work may run
A place where the task is cancelled
quiz.explain: await marks where the function may suspend and later resume, possibly after other tasks ran.

concepts.name: Packages, access control and tests
concepts.summary: Structure code into modules with Swift Package Manager, control visibility with access levels, and test with Swift Testing.
concepts.why: Real projects are split into packages and tested; access control decides what each module exposes.
concepts.body:
**Swift Package Manager** (SwiftPM) is Swift's built-in tool for building code, running tests and fetching the libraries your code needs (its **dependencies**). A package is a folder with a `Package.swift` file, a **manifest** written in Swift, that lists:

- **products** — what the package offers to others: libraries, or programs you can run (executables);
- **targets** — the separate parts of the code, each a **module** in its own folder under `Sources/` or `Tests/`;
- **dependencies** — other packages, given by their Git web address and a version requirement.

Common commands: `swift package init`, `swift build`, `swift run`, `swift test`. Xcode opens packages directly.

Each target is a module, and **access control** decides which code may use each thing you declare:

- `private` — only inside the enclosing type (and its extensions in the same file).
- `fileprivate` — the current file.
- `internal` — the whole module (the default).
- `package` — any module in the same package (Swift 5.9+).
- `public` — visible to code that imports the module; but outside the module, its classes can't be subclassed and its methods can't be overridden.
- `open` — public, plus subclassing and overriding allowed.

Design a small public API and keep everything else internal.

For tests, **Swift Testing** (bundled since Swift 6) uses `import Testing`, functions marked `@Test`, and the `#expect(...)` and `#require(...)` checks. These are macros (see the Macros lesson), so on failure they show the value of each part of the expression. `@Test(arguments:)` runs a test once per input, and tests run at the same time as each other by default. `@testable import MyLib` lets tests use internal declarations. The older XCTest framework still works alongside it.
takeaways: A package has products, targets (modules) and dependencies in `Package.swift`
Default access is `internal`; `public`/`open` export across modules
Swift Testing: `@Test`, `#expect`, parameterized `arguments:`
pitfalls: Forgetting that `public` classes can't be subclassed outside the module unless marked `open`.

quiz.q: What is the default access level of a declaration with no modifier?
quiz.explain: Without a modifier, a declaration is visible throughout its own module, which is internal.

concepts.name: async let, task groups and cancellation
concepts.summary: Run several child tasks at the same time with async let and task groups, and make long work stop when it's cancelled.
concepts.why: Running work in parallel with automatic clean-up and cancellation is what makes Swift concurrency safer than managing threads by hand.
concepts.body:
**Structured concurrency** means that tasks started inside another task — its **child tasks** — live inside a scope: the parent can't finish until all its children have, errors propagate up, and cancelling the parent cancels the children.

**`async let`** starts a child task immediately and lets you await its result later:

```swift
async let profile = loadProfile()
async let posts = loadPosts()
let page = try await Page(profile: profile, posts: posts)
```

Both loads run at the same time (in **parallel**). If you leave the scope without awaiting one, it is cancelled and awaited implicitly.

For a dynamic number of children, use a **task group**: `withTaskGroup(of:)` or `withThrowingTaskGroup(of:)`. Inside, `group.addTask { ... }` spawns children and `for await result in group` collects results **in completion order**. In a throwing group, the first error thrown out of the body cancels the remaining children.

Cancellation is cooperative (**cooperative cancellation**): cancelling a task only sets a flag. Long-running code must check it with `try Task.checkCancellation()` (throws `CancellationError`) or `Task.isCancelled`. Many system APIs such as `Task.sleep` and `URLSession` already throw when cancelled. Use `withTaskCancellationHandler` to react immediately, for example to stop older callback-based work.

`Task { }` and `Task.detached { }` create **unstructured** tasks that are not tied to the current scope; you must manage and cancel them yourself.
takeaways: `async let` and task groups run children in parallel within a scope
Group results arrive in completion order
Cancellation is cooperative — check it in long loops
pitfalls: Starting `Task { }` inside loops instead of a task group, losing cancellation and error propagation.

quiz.q: You cancel a task whose code never awaits or checks cancellation. What happens?
options: It keeps running to completion; only the isCancelled flag is set
quiz.explain: Swift cancellation is cooperative; code must check the flag or call APIs that do.

concepts.name: Actors and the main actor
concepts.summary: Protect changeable data with actors, run user-interface code on the main actor, and understand actor reentrancy.
concepts.why: Actors are Swift's built-in protection against data races, and @MainActor is how user-interface code stays on the main thread.
concepts.body:
An **actor** is a reference type that protects its changeable data: only one task at a time runs code that belongs to (is **isolated** to) the actor. From outside, accessing its properties or methods requires `await`, because you may have to wait your turn.

```swift
actor BankAccount {
    private var balance = 0
    func deposit(_ x: Int) { balance += x }
}
await account.deposit(10)
```

Inside the actor, code runs synchronously with direct access to its state. Mark a member `nonisolated` when it touches no changeable data (e.g. a `let` or a pure computed value), so callers don't need `await`.

A **global actor** is one actor that code from many different types can belong to. The important one is the **main actor**, `@MainActor`, which runs on the main thread, where all user-interface work must happen. Annotate view models, UI code and anything touching UIKit or AppKit with it. SwiftUI's `View` is main-actor isolated, and in Xcode 26 new app projects can default whole modules to the main actor.

Actors are **reentrant**: while an actor method is suspended at an `await`, other calls on the same actor can run. Facts you checked before an `await` may no longer hold after it, so re-check state afterwards and avoid splitting a read-modify-write around a suspension point.

Actors don't promise first-come, first-served order for calls, and they don't make work faster — they run it one call at a time. Keep actor methods short and move heavy pure computation out of them.
takeaways: Actor state is accessed one task at a time; outside callers `await`
`@MainActor` puts UI code on the main thread
Actors are reentrant — re-check state after every `await`
pitfalls: Assuming nothing changed in the actor across an `await` inside one of its methods.

quiz.q: Inside an actor method, you read `count`, then `await` a network call, then write `count + 1`. What is the risk?
options: Another call may have changed count during the await, so an update can be lost
None — actors run each method to completion atomically
quiz.explain: Actor reentrancy lets other calls run during suspension, so state read before an await may be stale.

concepts.name: Sendable and Swift 6 data-race safety
concepts.summary: Understand Sendable, how the Swift 6 language mode rejects data races at compile time, and how to fix common errors.
concepts.why: Swift 6 mode turns data-race warnings into errors, so every project migrating to it hits these diagnostics.
concepts.body:
In the **Swift 6 language mode**, the compiler proves your program free of data races: changeable data may only be touched from one **isolation domain** — an actor, the main actor, or a single task — at a time. Values crossing between domains must be safe to share, which the **`Sendable`** protocol expresses.

What is Sendable:

- Value types whose stored properties are all Sendable — automatically, for structs and enums that aren't public.
- Actors (they protect their own state).
- `final` classes with only immutable (`let`) Sendable properties.
- Closures marked `@Sendable`, which may only capture Sendable values and can't mutate captured vars.

A plain class with `var` properties is not Sendable. Passing it into `Task.detached`, an actor method, or capturing it in a `@Sendable` closure gives errors like "passing argument of non-sendable type ... risks causing data races".

Fixes, in order of preference:

- Make the type a struct, or make the class `final` with `let` properties.
- Isolate it: put it on `@MainActor` or turn it into an `actor`.
- Rely on **region-based isolation**: the compiler accepts a non-Sendable value passed across if it can prove the sender never uses it again.
- As a last resort, `@unchecked Sendable` when you protect state yourself with a lock such as `Mutex` from the Synchronization module.

Migrate module by module: enable strict concurrency checking (complete) in Swift 5 mode first, fix the warnings, then switch to `swiftLanguageModes: [.v6]`.
takeaways: Sendable = safe to share across isolation domains
Structs/enums of Sendable parts, actors and immutable final classes are Sendable
Prefer restructuring or isolation over `@unchecked Sendable`
pitfalls: Silencing every error with `@unchecked Sendable` or `nonisolated(unsafe)`, which just hides the races.

quiz.q: Which type is Sendable without extra work?
options: final class Cache { var dict: [String: Int] = [:] }
struct Point { var x: Int; var y: Int }
quiz.explain: A non-public struct whose stored properties are all Sendable is implicitly Sendable.

concepts.name: ARC, weak and unowned
concepts.summary: See how Swift frees class instances by counting references, and break retain cycles with weak and unowned references.
concepts.why: Retain cycles are the most common source of memory leaks in Swift apps, especially with closures and delegates.
concepts.body:
Swift manages class instances with **ARC**, automatic reference counting. Every normal (**strong reference**) to an instance adds one to its count; when the count drops to zero, the instance's `deinit` runs and its memory is freed straight away, at a predictable moment. There's no garbage collector running in the background.

The catch is a **retain cycle**: if A holds B strongly and B holds A strongly, neither count reaches zero, and both stay in memory forever — a **memory leak**. Break cycles with non-owning references:

- A **weak reference**, `weak var`, doesn't keep the object alive and becomes `nil` when it's freed, so it is always an optional `var`. Use it when the other object may go away first, e.g. a `delegate` or a child's reference to its parent.
- An **unowned reference**, `unowned`, doesn't keep the object alive and isn't optional, but using it after the object has been freed traps. Use only when the referenced object always outlives this one.

Closures are reference types and capture `self` strongly. A class that stores a closure that uses `self` forms a cycle. Break it with a **capture list** — square brackets at the start of the closure saying how to capture `self`:

```swift
onTap = { [weak self] in
    guard let self else { return }
    self.count += 1
}
```

Not every closure needs `[weak self]`: non-escaping closures, and escaping ones that are released after running (like a one-shot `Task` or animation), don't create lasting cycles.

Value types (structs, enums) aren't reference counted themselves, but any class references they contain are. Xcode's Memory Graph Debugger and the Leaks tool in Instruments (Apple's app for measuring programs) find cycles.
takeaways: ARC frees an object when its last strong reference disappears
`weak` becomes nil; `unowned` traps if used after free
Stored closures capturing `self` need `[weak self]`
pitfalls: Using `unowned` for an object that can actually be deallocated first, which crashes at run time.

quiz.q: Which declaration fits a delegate property (an object this one reports events to) that should not keep the delegate alive?
quiz.explain: A weak optional var doesn't own the delegate and safely becomes nil when it is freed.

concepts.name: some vs any: opaque and boxed types
concepts.summary: Choose between opaque types (some P) and existential types (any P) and understand their cost and limits.
concepts.why: SwiftUI's `some View` and modern APIs depend on this distinction, and it affects both performance and what compiles.
concepts.body:
Two ways to talk about "a value of some type conforming to `P`":

**Opaque types** — `some P` — mean one specific concrete type, chosen by the implementation and hidden from the caller. In a return position, `func makeShape() -> some Shape` must return the same concrete type on every path. The compiler knows the real type, so it can pick each method at compile time and make type-specific fast versions of the code. SwiftUI's `var body: some View` relies on this to keep huge nested view types hidden but fully typed. In a parameter, `some P` is just a generic parameter.

**Existential types** — `any P` — are a **box** that can hold a value of any conforming type, and the type can differ from value to value. You need them for collections that mix types, `[any Shape]`, or a stored property whose concrete type changes at run time. The cost: a value too big for the box's small built-in space is stored separately on the heap; each method call is looked up in a **witness table** (the type's list of where its protocol methods are); and the compiler can't make type-specific fast versions.

Limits of `any P`: when a protocol has `Self` or associated-type requirements, some members can't be used on the box directly (for example, `==` from `Equatable` between two `any Equatable`). Swift **opens** an existential when you pass it to a generic parameter, so `func check(_ x: some Equatable)` works with an `any Equatable` argument.

Rule of thumb: write `some` by default; use `any` when you truly need values of different types in the same place.
takeaways: `some P` = one fixed hidden type, statically dispatched
`any P` = a box that can hold different types, dynamic dispatch
Prefer `some`; use `any` to store values of different types together
pitfalls: Returning different concrete types from a `-> some P` function and wondering why it doesn't compile.

quiz.q: You need an array holding both Square and Circle values. Which element type works?
quiz.explain: Only an existential box can hold values of different concrete types in one array.

concepts.name: Property wrappers and result builders
concepts.summary: Write property wrappers to reuse the logic of storing a property, and understand the result builders behind SwiftUI's view code.
concepts.why: @State, @Binding and SwiftUI's declarative body are built on these two features.
takeaways: A property wrapper's `wrappedValue` handles get/set; `$name` is its projected value
Result builders turn statement lists into one value via `buildBlock` & co.
`@State` and `@ViewBuilder` are these features in SwiftUI
pitfalls: Putting `guard` or other unsupported statements inside a result-builder closure.

quiz.q: With `@State var count = 0` in SwiftUI, what is `$count`?
options: The wrapper's projected value, a Binding to count
quiz.explain: The $ prefix accesses the wrapper's projectedValue, which for @State is a Binding.

concepts.name: Isolation: regions, sending, nonisolated
concepts.summary: Reason about isolation inheritance, region-based isolation, the sending keyword and how async functions choose where to run.
concepts.why: Expert Swift 6 code relies on precise isolation rules to avoid both data races and needless switching between actors.
concepts.body:
Every piece of Swift code has a **static isolation**: an actor instance, a global actor such as `@MainActor`, or **nonisolated**. The compiler uses it to decide where code runs and what it may touch.

Inheritance rules worth knowing:

- `Task { }` inherits the isolation of where it is created (and captures the actor); `Task.detached { }` does not.
- Closures passed to non-`@Sendable` parameters inherit the caller's isolation.
- Members of a `@MainActor` type are main-actor isolated unless marked `nonisolated`.

**Where nonisolated async functions run** changed in Swift 6.2. Historically (SE-0338) they always moved to a shared pool of background threads. With the `NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault` upcoming feature, they run on the **caller's actor**, which removes many Sendable errors; annotate a function **`@concurrent`** to explicitly run it off the actor. The spelling `nonisolated(nonsending)` states the caller-inheriting behavior explicitly.

**Region-based isolation** (SE-0414) tracks groups of non-Sendable values. A value in a "disconnected" region — freshly created, and not reachable from any actor — can be transferred into another domain if the sender never uses it afterwards. The **`sending`** keyword (SE-0430) declares that a parameter or result is transferred this way: `func enqueue(_ job: sending Job)` accepts non-Sendable values the caller gives up.

`isolated` parameters (`func f(on actor: isolated MyActor)`) and `#isolation` let a function run on whatever actor it is passed, so general-purpose helpers don't have to switch actors.
takeaways: `Task {}` inherits isolation; `Task.detached {}` does not
`sending` transfers a non-Sendable value the caller stops using
Swift 6.2 can run nonisolated async code on the caller's actor; `@concurrent` opts out
pitfalls: Reaching for `Task.detached` to "go off the main thread" when a `@concurrent` or nonisolated function expresses the intent safely.

quiz.q: Why can a non-Sendable value be passed to an actor method declared with a `sending` parameter?
options: The compiler proves the caller no longer uses the value, so no sharing occurs
quiz.explain: Region-based isolation allows the transfer because the value's region is disconnected and the caller gives it up.

concepts.name: Copy-on-write and value-type performance
concepts.summary: Add copy-on-write to your own value types and avoid accidental copies, reference-count updates and the overhead of any-boxes.
concepts.why: Knowing what a value copy really costs is the difference between elegant and slow Swift.
concepts.body:
Standard collections are **copy-on-write** (CoW): copying an `Array` just copies a reference to a shared buffer (the memory holding the elements) and adds one to its reference count. The actual copy happens on the first mutation of a shared buffer, which checks `isKnownUniquelyReferenced`. If the buffer is unique, it mutates in place.

You can give your own value types this behavior by storing data in a private class and copying it before mutation when it's not unique:

```swift
if !isKnownUniquelyReferenced(&storage) { storage = storage.copy() }
```

Common performance traps:

- **Accidental copies**: holding a second reference while mutating (e.g. `let old = array; array.append(x)`) forces a full copy. Mutating through an intermediate variable copy, `var tmp = dict[key]!; tmp.append(x); dict[key] = tmp`, copies too; mutate in place with `dict[key, default: []].append(x)`.
- **Large structs** with many class-typed properties cost a reference-count update per property per copy. Grouping them into one CoW box helps.
- **Existentials** (`any P`) store values inside the box only up to three pointer-sized slots; larger ones go to the heap. Generic code with `some P` avoids this.
- **Non-final classes** and protocol requirements use dynamic dispatch; `final`, `private` and **whole-module optimization** let the compiler call methods directly instead.
- `@inlinable` exposes a function body across modules so generics can be specialized for callers.

Measure with Instruments (Time Profiler, Allocations) and build with `-O` (optimised); a **debug build** doesn't show real speed.
takeaways: CoW copies a shared buffer only on mutation, after a uniqueness check
Mutate in place; temporary copies defeat CoW
Use `final`, generics and `-O` builds when measuring performance
pitfalls: Benchmarking in Debug builds, where copies and dispatch are not optimized away.

quiz.q: `var a = [1, 2, 3]; var b = a; b[0] = 9` — when are the elements actually copied?
options: At `b[0] = 9`, because the buffer is shared
Never, a and b share storage forever
quiz.explain: Assignment shares the buffer; the first mutation of a non-unique buffer triggers the copy.

concepts.name: Noncopyable types and ownership
concepts.summary: Use ~Copyable types to model unique resources, and control ownership with borrowing, consuming and consume.
concepts.why: Noncopyable types give compile-time guarantees for files, locks and tokens that must exist exactly once.
concepts.body:
Normally every Swift type is implicitly `Copyable`. Since Swift 5.9 you can opt out with `~Copyable`, creating a **noncopyable type**: `struct FileHandle: ~Copyable`.
