Values of such a type have a single owner; assignment and passing **move** the value instead of copying it, and the compiler rejects any use of the old variable afterwards.

Noncopyable structs and enums can have a `deinit`, which runs exactly once when the owner's lifetime ends — ideal for closing a file descriptor or releasing a lock without a class or ARC.

Parameters of noncopyable type need an explicit **ownership** convention, saying who is responsible for the value:

- `borrowing` — the function gets read access temporarily; the caller keeps ownership.
- `consuming` — the function takes ownership; the caller can't use the value afterwards.
- `inout` — temporary exclusive mutable access.

The same words apply to methods: a `consuming func close()` ends the value's life, and inside it `discard self` skips the `deinit` when cleanup was already done manually.

The **`consume`** operator ends a variable's lifetime explicitly, even for copyable values: `let b = consume a` lets the optimizer avoid a copy and makes later use of `a` an error.

Generics can accept noncopyable types with `<T: ~Copyable>`, and since Swift 6 `Optional` and `Result` support them. Newer library types such as `Mutex`, `Atomic`, `Span` and `InlineArray` build on these features.
takeaways: `~Copyable` types have one owner; assignment moves them
Parameters use `borrowing`, `consuming` or `inout`
Noncopyable structs can have a `deinit`; `discard self` skips it
pitfalls: Forgetting the ownership modifier on a noncopyable parameter, which the compiler requires.

quiz.q: After `let b = a` where `a` is a ~Copyable struct, what happens when you call a method on `a`?
options: It works, both refer to the same value
a has been reset to its default value
quiz.explain: Assigning a noncopyable value moves it, and the compiler rejects any later use of the source.

concepts.name: Macros
concepts.summary: Use freestanding and attached macros, understand how they expand at compile time, and know what writing one involves.
concepts.why: @Observable, #Preview, #expect and @Model are macros; reading their expansions is essential for debugging.
concepts.body:
**Macros** (Swift 5.9+) generate code at compile time. Unlike C macros they work on the **syntax tree** (the compiler's structured view of your code), are type-checked, and only **add** code — they never delete or rewrite what you wrote.

Two families:

- A **freestanding macro** starts with `#` and produce an expression or declarations: `#Preview { ... }`, `#expect(a == b)`, `#URL("https://...")`-style validators.
- An **attached macro** starts with `@` and add to the declaration they're attached to. Roles include `@attached(member)` (add members), `peer` (add sibling declarations), `accessor` (add get/set), `memberAttribute`, and `extension` (add conformances). `@Observable` combines several roles to add observation storage and accessors to a class.

In Xcode, right-click a macro use and choose Expand Macro to see the generated code. This is the first thing to do when a macro-based API behaves unexpectedly.

A macro is declared in a library with `macro` and implemented in a separate compiler **plugin** — a small program the compiler runs while building — written with **SwiftSyntax**, Apple's library for reading and producing Swift code. The implementation is a type conforming to a protocol such as `ExpressionMacro` or `MemberMacro`, receiving the syntax node and returning new syntax. It runs in a sandbox, can't access the network or files, and should emit clear diagnostics instead of generating broken code. Running `swift package init --type macro` sets this all up, including tests using `assertMacroExpansion`.

Costs: SwiftSyntax adds build time, so prefer ordinary functions, generics or property wrappers when they suffice.
takeaways: Freestanding `#macro` makes expressions/declarations; attached `@Macro` adds to a declaration
Macros only add type-checked code; use Expand Macro to read it
Implementations are SwiftSyntax plug-ins running in a sandbox
pitfalls: Writing a macro for something a generic function or property wrapper already handles, paying build-time cost for nothing.

quiz.q: What can a Swift macro NOT do?
options: Delete or modify code you wrote
quiz.explain: Swift macros are additive: they insert new code but never remove or alter existing source.
